Can AI send emails for me?

Yes. The better question is whether you want it to press Send without you, and for most business email the answer is "not yet".

Checked 2026-11-21. Menus in other products change, so a label may differ slightly on your screen.

Short answer: yes. An AI email assistant can write emails for you today, and if it is connected to your mailbox it can send them too. For Outlook, Microsoft 365 Copilot drafts replies, summarizes long threads and suggests meeting times, and the full version needs a paid Copilot license on a work account. The safe way to use any of them is to have the AI prepare the email and approve each one yourself before it goes.

Three levels of "AI sends my email"

  1. It writes, you send. You ask a chat assistant for a draft and paste it into your email. This works anywhere and needs no set-up.
  2. It writes into your mailbox, you send. The assistant is connected to your email and leaves finished drafts addressed and ready. You open, check and send.
  3. It sends. The assistant sends from your address without you looking at each one.

Most of the value is at level 2. The email is written and addressed. All that is left is a look and a click.

What an AI email assistant for Outlook does

Most assistants for Outlook do the same few jobs:

  • Draft a reply from a short instruction, such as "tell her Thursday works and ask for the site address".
  • Summarize a long thread so you can see where it stands without reading 20 messages.
  • Suggest times for a meeting by looking at calendars.
  • Change the tone or length of something you wrote.

Here is an instruction that works well in any of them:

Write a short, polite reply to [name]. Say that [day and time] works for the visit at [address]. Ask them to confirm and to tell us if there is a gate code. Keep it under 80 words and sign off as [your name].

What Microsoft 365 Copilot in Outlook offers

Microsoft's own assistant is called Copilot. According to Microsoft's support page, Copilot in Outlook can:

  • pull the key points out of an email thread;
  • write a full draft from your instruction, using the thread for context;
  • create a meeting from an email thread, using the "Schedule with Copilot" button;
  • help sort your inbox and coach you on wording.

Microsoft says it works in new Outlook for Windows, Outlook for Microsoft 365 on Windows and Mac, and the Outlook phone apps. It needs a work or school account. It is not available on mailboxes that are not hosted on Exchange Online, and it cannot read encrypted emails. Microsoft's own advice is to review and edit anything it creates.

What license it needs

Microsoft's page on Copilot in Outlook says you need a Microsoft Copilot (work) license. For small businesses that is the paid add-on called Microsoft 365 Copilot Business, which you add to a Microsoft 365 business plan. At the time of writing, Microsoft's pricing page listed it at $21 per user per month on a yearly plan, with an offer price of $18. Prices and offers change, so check that page before you buy.

There is also a free Copilot Chat that comes with eligible Microsoft 365 plans. Microsoft's pages are not fully clear on how much of Outlook it covers, and they say a license is what gives Copilot full access to your emails, meetings and files. Ask whoever manages your Microsoft 365 account, or check Microsoft's current pages, before you promise yourself a feature.

What to look for in any tool that writes to customers

  • You review before it sends. Can you see and edit every email first?
  • It sends from your own mailbox. Replies should come back to you, and the email should look like yours.
  • What data it reads and keeps. Does it read your whole mailbox or only what the job needs? Is it stored, for how long, and is it used to train anything?
  • A "never write to" list. Can you tell it that certain people are never to be emailed, such as a customer in a dispute?
  • A record. Can you see what was sent, to whom and when?
  • One switch to stop everything.

If you send marketing email, the rules on unsubscribes are yours to follow, whoever writes the message.

Why drafts you approve beat emails sent unseen

  • The wrong person. Two customers with similar names, or an old address on file.
  • The wrong fact. AI can state an amount or a date with confidence and be wrong.
  • The wrong moment. A reminder sent an hour after the customer paid.
  • Too many. A mistake in the instruction can reach everyone on the list before you notice.

A draft you approve costs you a few seconds. An email sent unseen cannot be taken back. Keep a person in the loop until a job has gone right many times.

A safe way to start

  1. Pick one kind of email you send over and over, such as payment reminders or appointment confirmations.
  2. Have the AI prepare them and review every one for a few weeks.
  3. Turn each correction into a rule: "never chase this customer", "always include the invoice number".
  4. Only when you have stopped correcting, consider letting that one job send on its own.
